authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Meeting a new classmate
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Lina: Hello. Is this seat free?
Omar: Yes, it is. Please sit here.
Lina: Thank you. My name is Lina. What is your name?
Omar: I am Omar. I study engineering.
Lina: I study business. Are you from Bethlehem?
Omar: No, I am from Ramallah. And you?
Lina: I am from Bethlehem. Nice to meet you.
Omar: Nice to meet you too. Is this your first English class?

authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Talking about last weekend
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Lina: Did you enjoy the student book fair on Saturday?
Omar: Yes. I went with my cousin and bought two used books.
Lina: Were the books expensive?
Omar: No. They cost less than the new editions. One was about photography.
Lina: That sounds interesting. Did you stay all afternoon?
Omar: We left at three because my cousin had a family visit.
Lina: I missed the fair. I was helping my sister move.
Omar: There is another one next month. We can go together.

They could not find any books.

Omar: I would like two seats on the morning bus to Nablus, please.

authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Giving an opinion respectfully
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Lina: I think our study group should meet twice a week before the exam.
Omar: I see your point, but two long meetings may be difficult for students who work.
Lina: What if one meeting were online and only lasted thirty minutes?
Omar: That would help. We could use it to ask questions rather than repeat the lecture.
Lina: Agreed. The campus meeting could focus on solving practice problems.
Omar: We should ask everyone which evening works best before fixing a time.
Lina: I will send a short poll today. Could you prepare three practice problems?
Omar: Yes. Then we can review the plan after the first week.

choices: Working students may find two long meetings difficult.

understanding.prompt: What is the purpose of the online meeting?

vocabulary.meaning: Something that worries a person.
vocabulary.example: Use “concern” to describe an example from your own experience.

vocabulary.meaning: Give particular attention to.

vocabulary.meaning: Look at something again to see whether it works.

authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Preparing for a job interview
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Interviewer: Tell me about a time you worked with a team.
Omar: In a university project, our group had to present a simple energy-saving plan.
Interviewer: What was your responsibility?
Omar: I compared three options and summarized their costs. At first, I included too many technical details.
Interviewer: How did you deal with that?
Omar: I asked a classmate to listen to my explanation. Her questions helped me make the summary clearer.
Interviewer: What did you learn from the experience?
Omar: A good explanation depends on the audience. I now check that my main point is clear before adding detail.

choices: He included too many technical details.
He could not compare the costs.
He did not work with a team.
Removing every cost from the presentation.

authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Balancing different viewpoints
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Lina: Extending library hours could benefit students who have daytime jobs.
Omar: I support the idea, although staffing costs would have to be considered.
Lina: Perhaps we could trial longer hours during the exam period rather than throughout the year.
Omar: A trial would give us evidence, but attendance alone would not show whether the service was useful.
Lina: We could collect anonymous feedback as well as counting visits.
Omar: Provided the questions are neutral, that would strengthen the evaluation.
Lina: Let us propose a four-week pilot with a clear budget and a review date.
Omar: Agreed. We should also explain what would justify continuing or ending it.

choices: Some students work during the day.
All students prefer studying at night.
The library has no staffing costs.
It does not establish how useful the service was.
It proves that all visitors dislike the service.

understanding.prompt: What condition does Omar attach to feedback?

vocabulary.meaning: A limited test before a wider decision.

vocabulary.meaning: Not favoring a particular answer or viewpoint.

vocabulary.meaning: A systematic judgment of value or effectiveness.
vocabulary.example: Provided the questions are neutral, that would strengthen the evaluation.

authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Negotiating a shared outcome
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Omar: The team needs the rehearsal room on Thursday, but the music society has already booked it.
Lina: Could we negotiate a shorter session rather than asking them to cancel?
Omar: We need forty minutes to test the presentation equipment. They need an uninterrupted hour.
Lina: If we move our test to the start of the afternoon, they could keep their full session afterward.
Omar: That depends on whether the technician is available earlier.
Lina: I can check with her. We should make our proposal conditional on that confirmation.
Omar: Good. Let us also offer to reset the room so their rehearsal can start on time.
Lina: That makes the arrangement fairer. Both groups keep the time they actually need.

choices: Whether the room needs any equipment.

understanding.prompt: Why offer to reset the room?
choices: To help the other rehearsal start on time.
To shorten the other group’s session.

vocabulary.meaning: Only valid if another requirement is met.

authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Developing a nuanced argument
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Lina: The survey suggests that students who attend language workshops report greater confidence.
Omar: That is encouraging, but it does not establish that the workshops caused the improvement.
Lina: Students who were already motivated may have been more likely to attend.
Omar: Exactly. We should distinguish an association from a causal claim.
Lina: Would comparing participants’ confidence before and after the workshop address that limitation?
Omar: It would help, although a comparable non-participant group would make the interpretation stronger.
Lina: Then our recommendation should be a carefully evaluated pilot, rather than immediate expansion.
Omar: Yes. Acknowledge the promising findings while making the uncertainty explicit.

choices: An association between attendance and reported confidence.
That every student attended a workshop.
Already motivated students may be more likely to attend.
Participants were forbidden to report confidence.

vocabulary.meaning: A relationship that does not by itself prove cause.
vocabulary.example: Exactly. We should distinguish an association from a causal claim.

vocabulary.meaning: Showing that one thing produces another.
vocabulary.example: Exactly. We should distinguish an association from a causal claim.

vocabulary.meaning: Similar enough to support a fair comparison.
vocabulary.example: It would help, although a comparable non-participant group would make the interpretation stronger.

vocabulary.meaning: Stated clearly rather than implied.
vocabulary.example: Yes. Acknowledge the promising findings while making the uncertainty explicit.

authored_demonstration_lessons.title: Communicating a strategic recommendation
authored_demonstration_lessons.dialogue:
Omar: I recommend a phased introduction of the peer-mentoring scheme rather than a campus-wide launch.
Lina: Which constraint has most influenced that recommendation?
Omar: We can recruit mentors quickly, but consistent training and supervision would be harder to scale.
Lina: How would you judge whether the initial phase had succeeded?
Omar: I would combine participation data with confidential feedback and evidence that support needs were being addressed.
Lina: We also need safeguards so that enthusiasm does not substitute for qualified guidance.
Omar: Agreed. Mentors should know when to refer a student to an authorized professional.
Lina: Then present the proposal with clear boundaries, review criteria and conditions for expansion.

choices: Training and supervision are harder to scale than recruitment.
A campus-wide launch is already compulsory.
Mentors should refer issues requiring professional support.
Mentors should give every type of advice themselves.
Boundaries, review criteria and conditions for expansion.
Only a list of participation totals.

vocabulary.meaning: Introduced in planned stages.
vocabulary.example: I recommend a phased introduction of the peer-mentoring scheme rather than a campus-wide launch.

vocabulary.meaning: A limit affecting a decision.
vocabulary.example: Which constraint has most influenced that recommendation?

vocabulary.meaning: A measure that protects against a problem.
vocabulary.example: We also need safeguards so that enthusiasm does not substitute for qualified guidance.

vocabulary.meaning: Standards used to judge something.
vocabulary.example: Then present the proposal with clear boundaries, review criteria and conditions for expansion.
